equation.name: Temperature a world glows at, with its own heat
equation.formula:
t4 = (1 - A) * S / (4 * sigma) + F / sigma
T = sqrt(sqrt(max(t4, 0)))

S.name: starlight arriving on each square metre

source.text: Pearl, J. C. and Conrath, B. J. 1991, J. Geophys. Res. 96, 18921

explain.curious: Everything glows by its own warmth. A world warmed only by its star glows at the bare-ball temperature; Jupiter, Saturn and Neptune glow warmer because they are still losing the heat they were born with.
explain.science: Global energy balance: absorbed starlight spread over the whole sphere plus internal heat flux, radiated as a black body. This is the effective temperature Voyager and Cassini measured for the giants (Neptune 59.3 K, Pearl and Conrath 1991). The same block gives a star its effective temperature when the internal flux is its own luminosity over its surface.

equation.name: How much starlight a world sends back
equation.formula: X = A * pi * R * R * (Rs / d) * (Rs / d)

X.name: reflected light as an area of the star's face

source.text: Williams, D. R., NASA Planetary Fact Sheets, NSSDCA

explain.curious: Planets shine mostly by borrowed light. How much comes back depends on how big the world is, how pale it is, and how much of its star's light reaches it.
explain.science: A sphere of radius R at distance d intercepts πR² of a flux that, for a star of radius R* glowing at T*, is π B_λ(T*) (R*/d)². A fraction A (the Bond albedo) is sent back. Written as an effective area so the reflected spectrum is that area times the star's surface brightness. Grey albedo: real albedos vary with wavelength.

params.description: proton number density at 1 au, per cm³ (Sun: about 7)
radial field at 1 au, nT (Sun: about 3.5)

references: Parker, E. N. 1958, Dynamics of the interplanetary gas and magnetic fields, ApJ 128, 664: the spiral interplanetary field. doi:10.1086/146579

Kivelson, M. G. and Russell, C. T. (eds) 1995, Introduction to Space Physics, Cambridge University Press, chapter 9 (magnetopause stand-off from pressure balance, Chapman-Ferraro compression factor 2) https://www.cambridge.org/9780521457149
atoms.shown: ρ = n₁ m_p (1 au / d)², B_⊥ = B_r1 (1 au / d)² Ω d / v

equation.name: The star's wind where the world is
equation.formula:
x = au / d
rho = n1 * per_cc * m_p * x * x
v = vk * km
omega = 2 * pi / (Pd * day)
B = Br * nT * x * x * omega * d / v

explain.curious: Stars blow a thin wind of charged gas that carries their magnetic field out past the planets, wound into a spiral by the star's spin like water from a garden sprinkler.
explain.science: Parker's wind at constant speed: density falls as 1/d², the radial field as 1/d², and the azimuthal field B_φ = B_r Ω d / v as 1/d. B_φ is the part of the field across the flow that a magnetosphere intercepts. Defaults are solar values at 1 au; a star's own wind comes with stellar activity (O10).

checks.says: magnetic moment must be zero or more, got {}

references: Kivelson, M. G. and Russell, C. T. (eds) 1995, Introduction to Space Physics, Cambridge University Press, chapter 9 (magnetopause stand-off from pressure balance, Chapman-Ferraro compression factor 2) https://www.cambridge.org/9780521457149

equation.name: Where a world's magnetic field holds off the wind
equation.formula:
ram = rho * v * v
R = if M <= 0 or ram <= 0 then 0 else (mu0 * M * M / (8 * pi * pi * ram)) ^ (1/6)

M.name: strength of the world's magnet (dipole moment)

R.name: where the field holds the wind off

source.text: Kivelson, M. G. and Russell, C. T. (eds) 1995, Introduction to Space Physics, Cambridge University Press

explain.curious: A magnetic field holds the wind off like a bubble. Earth's bubble reaches about ten Earth radii towards the Sun; a world with no field has none.
explain.science: Pressure balance at the nose: the dipole field there, doubled by the currents on the boundary (Chapman-Ferraro), against the wind's ram pressure. Ignores plasma inside the bubble, which inflates Jupiter's to about twice this.

params.description: share of the intercepted magnetic power that comes out as radio (Zarka: about 2×10⁻³)

references: Zarka, P. 2007, Plasma interactions of exoplanets with their parent star and associated radio emissions, Planet. Space Sci. 55, 598: the radio-magnetic Bode's law, P_radio ≈ 2×10⁻³ of the incident magnetic power https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007P%26SS...55..598Z

Zarka, P., Treumann, R. A., Ryabov, B. P. and Ryabov, V. B. 2001, Magnetically-driven planetary radio emissions and application to extrasolar planets, Astrophys. Space Sci. 277, 293. doi:10.1023/A:1012221527425
atoms.shown: P = η (B_⊥² / μ₀) v π R_mp²  if R_mp > R, else 0

equation.name: Radio roar of a world's aurorae
equation.formula: P = if Rmp <= R then 0 else eta * B * B / mu0 * v * pi * Rmp * Rmp

Rmp.name: where the field holds the wind off

eta.name: share that comes out as radio

explain.curious: Magnetised planets are radio beacons. Jupiter is the loudest radio source in the sky after the Sun at long wavelengths; a world with no field is silent.
explain.science: The radio-magnetic Bode's law: every magnetised planet in the Solar System puts about the same small share of the wind's magnetic energy flux through its magnetosphere's cross-section into auroral radio. No magnetosphere (stand-off inside the body) gives no radio.

checks.says: magnetic moment must be zero or more, got {}

references: Treumann, R. A. 2006, The electron-cyclotron maser for astrophysical application, Astron. Astrophys. Rev. 13, 229: auroral radio is emitted near the local electron gyrofrequency f = eB/(2π m_e). doi:10.1007/s00159-006-0001-y

equation.name: Highest note of a world's radio aurorae
equation.formula:
B = mu0 * M / (2 * pi * R * R * R)
f = e / m_e * B / (2 * pi)

M.name: strength of the world's magnet (dipole moment)

f.name: highest radio frequency of its aurorae

source.text: Treumann, R. A. 2006, Astron. Astrophys. Rev. 13, 229

explain.curious: Auroral radio comes out at the rate electrons circle the field lines, so a stronger field means a higher top note. Jupiter's reaches tens of megahertz; Earth's only a few.
explain.science: Electron-cyclotron maser emission sits near the local gyrofrequency; its highest frequency is set by the strongest field, at the magnetic pole on the surface: B_pole = μ₀M / (2π R³) for a dipole. Real surface fields with multipoles go higher (Jupiter's 40 MHz cutoff).

positive.says: lobe width on the blue side
lobe width on the red side

references: Wyman, C., Sloan, P.-P. and Shirley, P. 2013, Simple analytic approximations to the CIE XYZ color matching functions, Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques 2(2), 1: the multi-lobe piecewise Gaussian fit, eq. 2 and table 1. https://jcgt.org/published/0002/02/01/
atoms.shown: g(λ) = exp(−½ ((λ − μ)/σ)²), σ = σ₁ below μ and σ₂ above

equation.name: One lobe of the eye's response to colour
equation.formula:
t = if x < mu then (x - mu) / s1 else (x - mu) / s2
g = exp(-t * t / 2)

mu.name: wavelength the lobe peaks at, in nanometres

s1.name: width of the lobe on its blue side, in nanometres

s2.name: width of the lobe on its red side, in nanometres

g.name: height of the lobe at this wavelength, 1 at its peak

source.text: Wyman, C., Sloan, P.-P. and Shirley, P. 2013, Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques 2(2), 1

explain.curious: The eye has three kinds of colour sensors. Their combined response to each wavelength is written as a few lopsided bell curves; the colour of any light follows from them.
explain.science: A piecewise Gaussian lobe with different widths either side of its peak; sums of these fit the CIE 1931 2° colour matching functions (lobe weights and shapes are data in the light pack).

checks.says: linear level must lie between 0 and 1, got {}

references: IEC 61966-2-1:1999, Multimedia systems and equipment, Colour measurement and management, Part 2-1: Default RGB colour space, sRGB (the transfer curve, section 5.2). https://webstore.iec.ch/publication/6169

equation.name: Screen level for a light level, as screens expect it
equation.formula: s = if v <= knee then slope * v else scale * v ^ (5/12) - offset

v.name: light level of one screen colour, 0 to 1, in proportion to light

knee.name: level below which the curve is a straight line

s.name: level sent to the screen, 0 to 1

source.text: IEC 61966-2-1:1999, Default RGB colour space, sRGB

explain.curious: Screens do not show levels in proportion to light: they expect a curve that spends more steps on dark shades, as eyes do.
explain.science: The sRGB transfer function (gamma encoding) from linear light to the encoded value.

checks.says: the cosine toward the viewer must lie between 0 (the limb) and 1 (the centre), got {}

references: Rybicki, G. B. and Lightman, A. P. 1979, Radiative Processes in Astrophysics, Wiley, section 1.8: a grey atmosphere in the Eddington approximation has T⁴ = (3/4) T_eff⁴ (τ + 2/3), and the light leaving at angle cos θ = μ comes from about optical depth μ (Eddington-Barbier). doi:10.1002/9783527618170

equation.name: How hot the layer you see is, from the centre of a disc to its edge

Teff.name: temperature of the glowing surface as a whole (effective temperature)

mu.name: cosine of the angle between the line of sight and straight out of the surface: 1 at the centre, 0 at the edge

T.name: temperature of the layer the light at that point comes from

source.text: Rybicki, G. B. and Lightman, A. P. 1979, Radiative Processes in Astrophysics

explain.curious: Look at a star's edge and you look in at a slant, so you see only its cooler upper layers. The edge is darker, and redder, than the middle.
explain.science: Eddington-Barbier: the emergent intensity at μ is about the source function at τ = μ; for a grey Eddington atmosphere that is the Planck function at T⁴ = (3/4) T_eff⁴ (μ + 2/3).

checks.says: Minnaert's k must lie between 0 and 2, got {}
the sunlight's cosine must lie between 0 and 1, got {}

references: Minnaert, M. 1941, The reciprocity principle in lunar photometry, Astrophys. J. 93, 403: reflected brightness goes as μ₀^k μ^(k−1), with k = 1 a Lambert surface. doi:10.1086/144279

equation.name: How bright a lit surface looks across its disc (Minnaert)

k.name: Minnaert's k: 1 for a matt surface, less for a hazy or dusty one that stays bright to the edge

mu0.name: cosine of the angle the sunlight arrives at

mu.name: cosine of the angle between the line of sight and straight out of the surface: 1 at the centre, 0 at the edge

b.name: brightness against a matt surface seen square on in full sun

explain.curious: A matt ball fades toward its edge; a hazy one, like a giant planet, stays bright almost to the rim. One number, k, says which.
explain.science: Minnaert's empirical law I/F = (I/F)₀ μ₀^k μ^(k−1), which keeps reciprocity; k = 1 is Lambert.

checks.says: a raindrop's refractive index must lie between 1 and 2 for a bow, got {}

references: Nussenzveig, H. M. 1977, The theory of the rainbow, Scientific American 236 (4), 116: Descartes' ray of minimum deviation after k internal reflections enters at cos² i = (n² − 1)/(k(k + 2)); the deviation is kπ + 2i − 2(k + 1)r, so water's primary bow is 42° and its secondary 51° from the antisolar point. doi:10.1038/scientificamerican0477-116
atoms.shown: cos² i = (n² − 1)/(k(k + 2)),  D = kπ + 2i − 2(k + 1) r,  bows at π − D₁ and D₂ − π

equation.name: How wide a rainbow is, from what is raining
equation.formula:
c1 = sqrt((n * n - 1) / 3)
i1 = atan2(sqrt(1 - c1 * c1), c1)
s1 = sin(i1) / n
r1 = atan2(s1, sqrt(1 - s1 * s1))
b1 = pi - (pi + 2 * i1 - 4 * r1)
c2 = sqrt((n * n - 1) / 8)
i2 = atan2(sqrt(1 - c2 * c2), c2)
s2 = sin(i2) / n
r2 = atan2(s2, sqrt(1 - s2 * s2))
b2 = 2 * pi + 2 * i2 - 6 * r2 - pi

n.name: refractive index of the falling drops

b1.name: radius of the primary bow round the point opposite the sun, as an angle in radians

b2.name: radius of the secondary bow, as an angle in radians

source.text: Nussenzveig, H. M. 1977, The theory of the rainbow, Scientific American 236 (4), 116

explain.curious: A rainbow is sunlight bent and bounced inside falling drops. How wide the bow is depends only on how strongly the liquid bends light, so rain of a different liquid makes a different-sized bow.
explain.science: Descartes' minimum-deviation ray after one and two internal reflections; the bows sit at the deviations' turning points.

a.source: Cox and Munk 1954, the clean-surface fit (eq. for σ² = σc² + σu²)

b.source: Cox and Munk 1954, the clean-surface fit (eq. for σ² = σc² + σu²)

checks.says: wind speed must be zero or more, got {}
a liquid's refractive index must lie between 1 and 3, got {}

references: Cox, C. and Munk, W. 1954, Measurement of the roughness of the sea surface from photographs of the sun's glitter, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 44, 838: the mean square slope of a clean sea, σ² = 0.003 + 5.12×10⁻³ W ± 0.004, W the wind at 12.5 m in m/s, fitted from aerial photographs of the glitter off Hawaii. doi:10.1364/JOSA.44.000838
Born, M. and Wolf, E. 1999, Principles of Optics, 7th edn, Cambridge University Press, section 1.5.3: at normal incidence a surface reflects ((n − 1)/(n + 1))² of the light, whatever its polarisation

equation.name: How wide and bright the sun's glint off a sea is

a.name: mean square slope of a calm sea

b.name: growth of the mean square slope with wind

s2.name: mean square slope of the waves (how far the glint spreads)

R0.name: share of light the liquid reflects straight back

source.text: Cox, C. and Munk, W. 1954, Measurement of the roughness of the sea surface from photographs of the sun's glitter, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 44, 838

explain.curious: Seen from space, a sea shows the sun as a soft bright patch: each little wave tilts a mirror toward you. More wind, more tilt, so the patch spreads wider and dimmer. A liquid that bends light more strongly reflects more of it.
explain.science: Gaussian facet slopes of variance σ² = 0.003 + 5.12×10⁻³ U (Cox and Munk's clean sea, fitted on Earth with the wind at 12.5 m; here read at 10 m and on other liquids as it stands, docs/fudges.md), with Fresnel's normal reflectance from the liquid's index; the renderer draws the facet BRDF from these two numbers.

references: Tape, W. 1994, Atmospheric Halos, Antarctic Research Series 64, American Geophysical Union: light through two faces of an ice crystal meeting at A is deviated least by D = 2 asin(n sin(A/2)) − A; 60° faces give the 22° halo, 90° faces the 46°. doi:10.1029/AR064

equation.name: How wide a halo round the sun or moon is, from the crystals in the air
equation.formula:
x = n * sin(A / 2)
D = 2 * atan2(x, sqrt(1 - x * x)) - A

A.name: angle between the two crystal faces the light passes through, in radians

D.name: radius of the halo round the sun, as an angle in radians

source.text: Tape, W. 1994, Atmospheric Halos, American Geophysical Union

explain.curious: Thin high cloud made of ice crystals can put a ring round the sun. Each crystal is a tiny prism, and the ring sits where its light is bent least.
explain.science: Minimum deviation of a prism of apex angle A; hexagonal ice gives 60° and 90° prisms.

series_below.source: Below this absorption size the closed form loses digits to cancellation, so its series 2w/3 - w^2/4 is used (exact to w^3)

phase_floor.source: Smallest phase shift kept, so a particle matching its surroundings (n = 1) scatters nothing instead of dividing by zero

checks.says: particle radius must be zero or more, got {}
wavelength must be more than zero, got {}
the imaginary refractive index must be zero or more, got {}

references: van de Hulst, H. C. 1957, Light Scattering by Small Particles, Wiley (Dover 1981), sections 11.22 and 11.23: anomalous diffraction, extinction for an absorbing sphere and absorption. doi:10.1063/1.3060205
atoms.shown: ρ = 2x(n−1), tan β = k/(n−1), Q_ext = 2 − 4e^(−ρ tan β)(cos β/ρ) sin(ρ−β) − 4e^(−ρ tan β)(cos β/ρ)² cos(ρ−2β) + 4(cos β/ρ)² cos 2β; Q_abs = 1 + 2e^(−w)/w + 2(e^(−w)−1)/w², w = 4xk; ω = 1 − Q_abs/Q_ext

equation.name: How much light a particle scatters rather than absorbs
equation.formula:
x = 2 * pi * r / lam
rho = max(2 * x * abs(n - 1), phase_floor)
beta = atan2(k, abs(n - 1))
c = cos(beta) / rho
e = exp(-rho * tan(beta))
Qe = 2 - 4 * e * c * sin(rho - beta) - 4 * e * c * c * cos(rho - 2 * beta) + 4 * c * c * cos(2 * beta)
w = 4 * x * k
Qa = if w < series_below then 2 * w / 3 - w * w / 4 else 1 + 2 * exp(-w) / w + 2 * expm1(-w) / (w * w)
om = if Qe <= 0 then 1 else clamp(1 - Qa / Qe, 0, 1)

n.name: refractive index of the particle's material (real part)

k.name: how strongly the material absorbs (imaginary part of the refractive index)

series_below.name: absorption size below which the series is used

Qe.name: light taken out of the beam, per particle's cross-section

om.name: share of the light taken out that is scattered, not absorbed

source.text: van de Hulst, H. C. 1957, Light Scattering by Small Particles

explain.curious: A haze particle either bounces light on or soaks it up. Tholin soaks up blue far more than red, so Titan's haze sends back orange.
explain.science: Anomalous diffraction for a sphere much larger than the wavelength with a refractive index near one: extinction from the phase lag through it, absorption from the path through it; the single-scattering albedo is one minus their ratio.

thin_below.source: Below this the layer is taken as conservative (no absorption), where the closed form is 0/0; the conservative form is its limit

checks.says: optical depth must be zero or more, got {}
single-scattering albedo must lie between 0 and 1, got {}
asymmetry must lie between -1 and 1, got {}

references: Bohren, C. F. 1987, Multiple scattering of light and some of its observable consequences, Am. J. Phys. 55, 524 (two-stream reflectance of a slab, R = (1 - g)τ / (2 + (1 - g)τ) when nothing is absorbed). doi:10.1119/1.15109

Meador, W. E. and Weaver, W. R. 1980, Two-stream approximations to radiative transfer in planetary atmospheres, J. Atmos. Sci. 37, 630 (the general solution for an absorbing slab). doi:10.1175/1520-0469(1980)037<0630:TSATRT>2.0.CO;2
atoms.shown: γ₁ = 1 − ω(1+g)/2, γ₂ = ω(1−g)/2, κ = √(γ₁² − γ₂²); R = γ₂ tanh κτ / (κ + γ₁ tanh κτ), T = κ sech κτ / (κ + γ₁ tanh κτ)

equation.name: Light a layer of cloud or haze sends back and lets through
equation.formula:
g1 = 1 - om * (1 + g) / 2
g2 = om * (1 - g) / 2
kk = sqrt(max(g1 * g1 - g2 * g2, 0))
e = exp(-2 * kk * tau)
th = (1 - e) / (1 + e)
sh = 2 * exp(-kk * tau) / (1 + e)
R = if kk * tau < thin_below then g2 * tau / (1 + g1 * tau) else g2 * th / (kk + g1 * th)
T = if kk * tau < thin_below then 1 / (1 + g1 * tau) else kk * sh / (kk + g1 * th)

tau.name: optical depth of the layer straight down

om.name: share of the light taken out that is scattered, not absorbed

g.name: how far forward the particles scatter (0 alike every way, 1 straight on)

thin_below.name: absorption depth below which the layer is taken as not absorbing

R.name: share of the light the layer sends back

T.name: share of the light the layer lets through

source.text: Meador, W. E. and Weaver, W. R. 1980, J. Atmos. Sci. 37, 630, with Bohren 1987's coefficients
source.where: the two-stream solution for a homogeneous layer

explain.curious: A thick cloud sends most light back and lets little through; one that also absorbs sends back less, and what it sends back takes on the colour it absorbs least.
explain.science: Two-stream radiative transfer for a homogeneous slab of scatterers with single-scattering albedo ω and asymmetry g, coefficients as in Bohren 1987 so a conservative slab matches weather.ts; diffuse reflectance and transmission, no floor.

references: Luminet, J.-P. 1979, Image of a spherical black hole with thin accretion disk, A&A 75, 228 https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1979A%26A....75..228L
Cunningham, C. T. and Bardeen, J. M. 1973, The optical appearance of a star orbiting an extreme Kerr black hole, ApJ 183, 237 https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1973ApJ...183..237C
Misner, C. W., Thorne, K. S. and Wheeler, J. A. 1973, Gravitation, W. H. Freeman (Schwarzschild geometry, chapters 25 and 31) https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1973grav.book.....M

equation.name: How much bluer or redder the light from one point of a disc arrives
equation.formula:
x = r / rg
bb = b / rg
z1 = if x <= 3 then 0 else (1 - bb * sin(i) * sin(al) / sqrt(x^3)) / sqrt(1 - 3 / x)
g = if z1 <= 0 then 0 else 1 / z1

r.name: distance of the glowing point from the centre

b.name: impact parameter of the ray that reaches the viewer

i.name: angle between the line of sight and the disc's axis, radians (0 face on)

al.name: angle round the picture from the disc's axis as seen, towards the viewer's left, radians

source.text: Luminet 1979, eq. 19 (sign of α as here); Cunningham and Bardeen 1973
source.where: gas on circular orbits round a mass that does not spin, viewer far away; disc turning anticlockwise seen from the viewer's side

explain.curious: Gas near a black hole orbits at up to half the speed of light. The side coming towards you looks bluer and far brighter, the side going away redder and dimmer, and all of it is reddened by climbing out of the hole's pull.
explain.science: 1 + z = u^t (1 − Ω λ): u^t = (1 − 3M/r)^(−½) for a circular orbit (gravity and time dilation together), Ω = (M/r³)^½, and λ = b sin i sin α the photon's angular momentum about the disc's axis, which is conserved along the bent ray, so the same expression serves the direct image, the arch and the thin ring. A glowing ring at T is then seen as glowing at gT, with total brightness times g⁴.
